treatment.proposition: An intervening and independent wrongful act of a third person that produces the injury is treated as the proximate cause and insulates the defendant's negligence, unless the defendant had reasonable grounds for apprehending that the wrongful act would be committed; foreseeability of intervening criminal acts is usually for the factfinder, and the court decides it when the evidence is plain and undisputable (300 Ga. at 841-843).
treatment.report:
CASE: Goldstein, Garber & Salama, LLC v. J. B., 300 Ga. 840, 797 S.E.2d 87 (2017) (S16G0744) [Verified (heavyweight)]
PROPOSITION CHECKED: An intervening and independent wrongful act of a third person that produces the injury is treated as the proximate cause and insulates the defendant's negligence, unless the defendant had reasonable grounds for apprehending that the wrongful act would be committed; foreseeability of intervening criminal acts is usually for the factfinder, and the court decides it when the evidence is plain and undisputable (300 Ga. at 841-843).
JURISDICTION: Georgia state courts (Supreme Court of Georgia; Court of Appeals of Georgia)
STATUS: VALID, confidence moderate
DIRECT HISTORY: Docket S16G0744 holds cluster 5749642 and a same-day "FINAL COPY" (cluster 10354572) with identical Division 1 text. Reconsideration denied March 30, 2017. On remand the Court of Appeals vacated its opinion and adopted this one: Goldstein, Garber & Salama, LLC v. J. B., 344 Ga. App. 110, 808 S.E.2d 913 (2017) [Not validated]. No further appeal located.
ADVERSE TREATMENT: None located. Jordan v. Everson, 302 Ga. 364, 365, 806 S.E.2d 533 (2017) [Not validated] explains the rule: "there is no requirement in Georgia that an intervening act be 'wrongful or negligent' to break the causal chain," and the Court of Appeals "read too much into that sentence" from Goldstein, which addressed "an indisputably wrongful act." Cleveland v. Team RTR2, LLC (Ga. Ct. App. Feb. 3, 2021) [Not validated] distinguished Goldstein because it "did not involve previous similar crimes on the premises." The screen's Tier B and C hits are quotations: Maynard v. Snapchat, Inc., 313 Ga. 533 (2) (2022) [Not validated] follows the rule at 841 alongside Jordan; its "questions" hit at 843 sits in a dissent joined by LaGrua, J. Johnson v. Avis Rent A Car Sys., LLC, 311 Ga. 588, 592-593, 858 S.E.2d 23 (2021) [Screened (lightweight)] quotes 841-842 and applies it. Wang v. Dukes (Ga. Ct. App. June 27, 2023) [Not validated] cites 841 for the four elements. "Judgment reversed" in Maynard v. Snapchat, Inc. (Ga. Ct. App. Jan. 25, 2023) [Not validated] reverses the trial court's dismissal and follows 841-842.
AT-RISK FINDINGS: Upstream clean: Ontario Sewing Mach. Co. v. Smith, 275 Ga. 683 (2002); Munroe v. Universal Health Servs., Inc., 277 Ga. 861 (2004); Johnson v. American Nat'l Red Cross, 276 Ga. 270 (2003); Atlanta Obstetrics & Gynecology Grp. v. Coleman, 260 Ga. 569 (1990) [all Not validated]. Two context limits. (1) Ga. CVS Pharmacy, LLC v. Carmichael, 316 Ga. 718 (II) (2023) [Not validated] places crime foreseeability in premises cases within the OCGA § 51-3-1 duty, keeps Goldstein at 842 for proximate cause, and lets the court rule "where no rational juror could determine the issue in favor of the non-moving party." (2) OCGA §§ 51-3-50 and 51-3-51 (Ga. L. 2025, p. 19, § 6, SB 68, eff. April 21, 2025) set statutory foreseeability proof for negligent-security claims against owners, occupiers, and security contractors. Neither reaches Goldstein's professional-supervision setting.
RECENT APPLICATION: Venetian Hills Apartments, LLC v. Hughes, No. A25A1091 (Ga. Ct. App. Oct. 31, 2025) [Not validated], citing 300 Ga. at 842 to hold "the jury was authorized to find that an intervening act did not insulate the landlord from liability" (judgment vacated on a charge error).
IF UNUSABLE, WHAT REPLACES IT: n/a. Cite Jordan v. Everson with Goldstein whenever the memo states the rule, so the word "wrongful" reads as descriptive.
COVERAGE: citing_count 35; 35 listed by the citeCount sweep; 29 read in passage by the screen plus 20 search_document passages on invalidating-court citers and word-search hits; full or chunked reads of Jordan, Maynard (ga and Ga. App.), Wang, Carmichael, Venetian Hills, Cleveland, the final copy, and the remand; Johnson v. Avis from saved text. Invalidating courts swept: ga, scotus (5 Supreme Court of Georgia decisions, no SCOTUS citers). Word searches: case name, reporter cites, case name with negative-treatment terms. Legs 1 to 4 run; Leg 4 semantic query (ga, since 2016) and Georgia Commons. Jordan and Carmichael surfaced only through word searches; the cites: sweep missed both, and the scorer did not flag Jordan's "did not overrule" or Cleveland's "distinguishable." About 53 CourtListener requests. Confidence caps at moderate: no tiered ranking, no curated flag co-occurrence, no truncation reporting. The user's manual KeyCite remains required.

request.issue: Issue 3: intervening criminal act of a third party and proximate cause (Georgia)
request.proposition: whether and when a third party's intentional crime is a superseding cause that relieves the original negligent actor of liability, and the foreseeability exception
request.free_sources_tried: CourtListener full-text search of Supreme Court of Georgia and Court of Appeals of Georgia opinions for the Restatement (Second) of Torts superseding-cause sections (sections 440, 442, 448, 449) returned one opinion, SecureAlert, Inc. v. Boggs, 815 S.E.2d 156 (Ga. Ct. App. 2018), which cites section 448 in a footnote without applying it. The Georgia cases read (Goldstein, Garber & Salama, LLC v. J. B., 300 Ga. 840 (2017); Johnson v. Avis Rent A Car System, LLC, 311 Ga. 588 (2021)) state the rule through Ontario Sewing Machine Co. v. Smith and do not cite the Restatement for it.
